title.en: Hoori Drowns and Spares His Elder Brother with the Tide Jewels
title.zh: 火遠理命以潮滿潮涸珠懲戒兄長

region.en: Sea-crossing and shore of Himuka, Tsukushi (Kyushu) (symbolic pin for the sea-path between the Sea-Plain and the Upper Land)
region.zh: 日向筑紫海岸與海路（象徵性定位）

summary.en: Returning to the Upper Land from the Sea-Deity's palace, Hoori rides home on a one-fathom crocodile in a single day and leaves his stiletto girded on its neck, whence the creature is called the Deity Blade-Possessor. He hands back the fish-hook exactly as instructed, and when his sea-luck elder brother attacks him he first drowns him with the tide-flowing jewel, then releases him with the tide-ebbing jewel, until the brother bows and becomes his guard by day and night. The origin of the Hayabito court jesters' drowning-antics is traced to this humiliation.
summary.zh: 火遠理命騎一尋鱷魚一日返家，留短劍於鱷頸，故稱劍持神。他依海神教導交還魚鉤，兄長海幸（火照）怒而攻之，火遠理命先以潮滿珠淹沒，再以潮涸珠救活，直至兄長臣服，日夜侍衛。隼人朝廷弄臣之舞即源於此辱。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Sea-Deity summoned all the crocodiles together and asked which of them would escort his son-in-law, the august child of the Heaven's-Sun-Height, back to the Upper Land, and in how many days. One crocodile just one fathom long promised to make the journey in a single day, and the Sea-Deity chose him: carry him respectfully, he said, and do not alarm him while you cross the middle of the sea. So the god seated Hoori on the crocodile's head and saw him off. The crocodile kept his word and delivered Hoori home in one day. As the creature turned to go back, Hoori untied the stiletto girded at his own waist, set it on the crocodile's neck, and sent him away with that mark of honour. Ever since, the one-fathom crocodile has been called the Deity Blade-Possessor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 210-211 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hoori now handed the fish-hook back to his elder brother exactly as the Sea-Deity had instructed. From that day the elder brother grew poorer and poorer, and in fresh savagery came to attack him. As the attack began, Hoori put forth the tide-flowing jewel and drowned him; when he cried out in grief, Hoori put forth the tide-ebbing jewel and let him live. Thus harrassed, the sea-luck brother bowed his head and promised: henceforward I will be your guard by day and by night, and respectfully serve you. Down to the present day, says the record, the drowning-brother's posturings are ceaselessly served up before the court - for the Hayabito, descendants of the Prince of Fire-Shine, still perform before the sovereign the dances that mimic the antics their divine ancestor went through while the waters rose about him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 211-212 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Toyotama-hime's Seaside Childbirth and the Crocodile Reveal
title.zh: 豐玉姬海濱產房化鱷之秘

region.en: Sea-shore at the wave-limit of Himuka, Tsukushi (Kyushu) (symbolic pin on the parturition-hall of cormorants' feathers)
region.zh: 日向筑紫海濱波限鵜葺草葺不合命誕生地（象徵性定位）

summary.en: The Sea-Deity's daughter Toyotama-hime, pregnant by Hoori, refuses to bear the heavenly child in the sea-plain and comes ashore, where a parturition-hall roofed with cormorants' feathers is hastily built. Unable to wait for the thatch, she enters it in travail and forbids her husband to watch, for a woman of another land takes her native shape in childbirth. Hoori peeps at the moment of delivery and sees a crocodile eight fathoms long writhing on the floor; he flees in terror, and the shamed sea-bride abandons her child, closes the sea-path, and returns to her father's realm - though love draws her back once more with a song.
summary.zh: 海神女豐玉姬懷火遠理命之子，不肯於海中原產，遂至陸上以鵜羽葺屋待產。未及葺成，陣痛難忍，遂入產房，囑夫勿窺：異國婦人生產必復本形。火遠理命偷窺，見八尋鱷魚爬行蠕動，驚逃。豐玉姬知之，羞慚棄子，閉海路而去；然情難自禁，託妹玉依姬獻歌一次。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Toyotama-hime herself came to wait upon Hoori and told him the time of delivery was near: I am already with child, she said, but the august child of a Heavenly Deity ought not to be born in the Sea-Plain, and so I have come to you. On the very limit of the waves she began a parturition-hall, thatching it with cormorants' feathers. Before the thatch was half finished the urgency of her womb could no longer be restrained, and she went in to be delivered. At the door of her labour she made her husband swear: whenever a foreign woman is delivered, she takes the shape of her native land; so I too shall now take my native shape. Pray, do not look upon me!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 212 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hoori found the words strange, and at the very moment of delivery he could not help stealing a look. There, writhing and crawling on the floor of the hall, was a crocodile eight fathoms long. Terrified, he fled. Toyotama-hime knew at once that he had peeped; filled with shame she abandoned the child she had just borne and said: I had wished always to come and go across the sea-path between us; but your having looked upon my true shape leaves me very shame-faced. So she closed the sea-boundary and went down again to the sea. The son she left behind was named Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-Limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely, after the unfinished roof of his birth-hall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 212-213 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Though angry at her husband's wish to peep, the sea-bride could not restrain her loving heart. At the time her younger sister Jewel-Good-Princess came to nurse the abandoned child, Toyotama-hime entrusted to her a song to be presented to Hoori, and he answered with a song in return - the parting exchange of the sea and the land. The child, Hoori's heir, dwelt thereafter in the palace of Takachiho, and in time wedded his maternal aunt Jewel-Good-Princess: from that marriage the line of the future emperors of Yamato descends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 213-215 (1882); not verbatim.

region.en: Yamato plain at Unebi-Kashibara (Nara); route of the expedition from Himuka in Kyushu through Tsukushi and Kibi to Yamato
region.zh: 畝傍橿原宮（奈良）；東征路線自日向經筑紫、吉備至大和

summary.en: The two princes Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko (the future Emperor Jimmu) and Itsuse leave Himuka to seek a land from which to govern the empire peaceably. Itsuse dies of an arrow-wound from Nagasune-biko, declaring it wrong to fight facing the sun; Jimmu's whole army is struck down by a phantom bear in Kumano until a cross-sword drops through the roof of Takakurazhi's storehouse in answer to a dream of the gods. Guided by the crow of eight feet sent from heaven, Jimmu recruits earth-deities, traps the traitor Ukashi in his own pitfall, has eighty tailed earth-spiders slain at a banquet song, and receives the heavenly regalia from Nigi-hayabi before ruling the empire from Kashibara.
summary.zh: 神渟名川耳尊（神武天皇）與兄五瀨命自日向東征，欲擇善地治天下。五瀨命中長髓彥毒箭，言不可面日而戰，傷重而亡。熊野遇巨熊幻影，全軍昏倒；高倉下夢得建御雷神自屋頂落入之劍，軍乃復甦。天照大神與高皇產靈遣八咫烏引路，收服土神，誅兄狹兄磯城，設伏誅八十梟帥，邇藝速命獻天璽瑞寶，遂於畝傍橿原宮即位治天下。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), foundational narrative of the imperial line; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology, not as endorsement of any imperial or nationalist reading.

passages.text: In the palace of Takachiho the two deities Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko and his elder brother Itsuse took counsel: dwelling in what place shall we most quietly carry on the government of the empire? It were best, they decided, to go east. They left Himuka and progressed to Tsukushi, where at Usa in the land of Toyo the natives Usa-tsu-hiko and Usa-tsu-hime built a one-legged raised platform and served them a great banquet. They dwelt a year at Wokada in Tsukushi, seven years at Takeri in the land of Agi, and eight years at Takashima in Kibi. Setting out again, they met in the Hayasuhi Channel a man riding the carapace of a tortoise and raising his wings as he angled. Questioned, he answered: I am an Earthly Deity; I know the sea-path well, and I will respectfully serve you. They drew him into the vessel with a pole and named him Sawo-ne-tsu-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 216-218 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Passing the Namihaya Crossing they brought up at the haven of Shirakata, where Nagasune-biko of Tomi raised an army to meet them. The brothers disembarked behind shields taken from their vessel - the place was named Tadetsu for it - and in the fighting Itsuse was pierced in the hand by the Prince of Tomi's hurtful arrow. He cried out: it is not right for me, an august child of the Sun-Deity, to fight facing the sun; that is why this wretched villain's hand has stricken me. I will turn and smite him with my back to the sun. Making a circuit by the south, he reached the sea of Chinu and washed the blood from his hand; then at the river-mouth of Wo in the land of Ki he lamented - ah, that I should die stricken by a wretched villain's hand! - and expired as a valiant man. His mausoleum is on Mount Kama in Ki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 218-219 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Progressing round to the village of Kumanu, Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko met a great bear that came out of the mountain and vanished into it again. At that instant the prince suddenly fainted away, and his whole army fell prostrate. Then Takakurazhi of Kumanu came bearing one cross-sword and presented it to the fallen prince, who rose at once saying: how long I have slept! - and the savage deities of the mountains of Kumanu fell cut down of themselves while the bewildered army awoke. Takakurazhi explained that in a dream the Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity and the High Integrating Deity had summoned the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity and charged him: the Central Land of Reed-Plains is painfully uproarious and our august children must be ill at ease; you who specially subdued that land must descend. He answered: I will not descend myself, but I will send down the cross-sword wherewith I subdued the land - perforate the ridge of Takakurazhi's storehouse and drop it through. Searching at dawn, Takakurazhi had found the sword exactly so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 220-222 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The High Integrating Deity commanded again in dream: make no progress into the interior, for the savage deities are many; I will send from heaven a crow eight feet long, and you shall follow it. Following the crow, the prince reached the Yeshinu river, questioned a fisher of a weir and a man with a tail who came from a shining well, then another tailed man who pushed the cliffs apart to meet him - all Earthly Deities come to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deity. At Uda, the elder brother Ukashi shot a whizzing barb at the crow-messenger and built a great palace with a pitfall inside; his younger brother betrayed him. The generals Michi-no-Omi and Ohokume, grasping their sword-hilts and fixing arrows, drove the elder Ukashi into the palace he had built, where he fell into his own gin and died, and they cut him in pieces at Uda-no-Chihara. At the great cave of Osaka eighty tailed earth-spider bravoes were slain: the prince set one butler with a sword for each, and when he sang the signal-song, all drew together and cut them down. Having subdued the savage deities and extirpated the unsubmissive people - Nigi-hayabi had come down from heaven to present the heavenly symbols - Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko dwelt at the palace of Kashibara near Unebi and ruled the Empire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 222-231 (1882); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Kojiki's forty-seventh section turns from the sea-born line of Hoori and Toyotama-hime to the beginning of the imperial line itself. Two sons of that line, Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko - later honoured as Emperor Jimmu, the first human sovereign of Japan - and his elder brother Itsuse, dwell in the palace of Takachiho in Himuka (southern Kyushu) and take counsel together: by dwelling in what place shall we most quietly carry on the government of the empire? The answer is to go east, toward the Central Land of Reed-Plains, the Yamato plain that the heavenly deities were said to have subdued long before. The eastward progress begins as a slow, ritual migration: the brothers land at Usa in Toyo, where the local chieftains Usa-tsu-hiko and Usa-tsu-hime raise a one-legged platform and serve a great banquet; they spend a year at Wokada in Tsukushi, seven years at Takeri in Agi, and eight years at Takashima in Kibi, gathering strength and local allies as they go. On the sea they meet a miraculous old man riding the shell of a tortoise and raising his wings as he angles; he declares himself an Earthly Deity, offers to serve them, and is drawn aboard and named Sawo-ne-tsu-hiko - in the Nihongi this figure is the god Shiotsuchi, the pilot of the expedition.

The first open resistance comes at the haven of Shirakata, where Nagasune-biko, the Long-Nosed Prince of Tomi, raises an army to bar the way. The brothers disembark behind shields taken from their vessel, giving the beach its name, Tadetsu, the place of shields. In the fight Itsuse is pierced in the hand by Nagasune's arrow, and the wound kills him, but only after he pronounces the expedition's solar logic: I am an august child of the Sun-Deity, he says; it is not right to fight facing the sun - that is why the wretched villain's hand has stricken me. Henceforward I will smite him with my back to the sun. The army turns and approaches from the south; Itsuse washes the blood from his hand in the sea of Chinu, and dies at the river-mouth of Wo in the land of Ki, lamenting that a heaven-born prince should fall by a villain's arrow. His death teaches the campaign's central rule - the eastward march must move with, never against, the light of the ancestress the Sun-Deity Amaterasu.

Kumano brings the deepest crisis. A great bear steps out of the mountain and vanishes back into it, and at the sight Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko faints away; his whole army falls prostrate as if the god's power had struck them down. Deliverance comes not through force but through a dream. Takakurazhi of Kumanu tells how the Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity (Amaterasu) and the High Integrating Deity (Takamimusubi) summoned the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity - Takemikazuchi, the thunder-god who had wrested the land from the earthly deities - and charged him to descend and quiet the uproarious Central Land for their august children. Takemikazuchi answers that he will not descend himself but will send down the cross-sword with which he subdued the land, dropping it through the ridge of Takakurazhi's storehouse roof. At dawn Takakurazhi finds the sword and presents it to the prince. At its acceptance the army revives, and the savage mountain deities of Kumano fall cut down of themselves. The sword is the futsu-no-mitama, the quelling-spirit blade whose cult later centres on Kashima shrine.

A second dream instructs the campaign's method: make no progress into the interior, for the savage deities are many; I will send from heaven a crow eight feet long, and you shall follow it. This is the yatagarasu, the divine sun-crow that guides Jimmu up the Yeshinu river, past a fisher of a weir and two tailed earth-deities, one emerging from a shining well and another from a cleft he pushes apart, each announcing that he has come to serve the august son of the Heavenly Deity. The crow is still the emblem of the Kumano shrines.

Human foes remain. In Uda the elder brother Ukashi shoots a whizzing barb at the crow-messenger to turn it back, then pretends submission and builds a great palace with a pitfall inside. His younger brother betrays the plan to Jimmu. The generals Michi-no-Omi and Ohokume seize Ukashi the Elder, revile him, and drive him - grasping sword-hilts, playing with spears, arrows set to their bows - into the palace he built to deceive his sovereign; he falls into the gin he set for another and is cut to pieces at Uda-no-Chihara. The prince then bestows on his army the great banquet the loyal younger brother had prepared, singing a song of contempt for the traitor. At the great cave of Osaka, eighty tailed earth-spider bravoes await him; he sets a girded butler of his own beside each of them, and when he sings the cue-song they draw their swords simultaneously and slaughter the whole band. Songs are the expedition's war-signals: further verses mark the assault on the Prince of Tomi and the defeat of the Shiki brothers.

The expedition ends in submission and investiture. Nigi-hayabi, who had followed from heaven, waits on Jimmu and presents the heavenly symbols - the mirror, sword, and jewels of the regalia - and the country is quiet. Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko weds Princess Ahira in Himuka and later the divine-born I-suke-yori-hime of Miwa, and rules the Empire from the palace of Kashibara near Unebi. The record counts his life at one hundred and thirty-seven years and fixes his mausoleum on the northern side of Mount Unebi - the grave still claimed as Jimmu's tomb. The narrative works as charter myth for the imperial eastward conquest: every obstacle is overcome not by mere force but by solar alignment, dream-oracles, a god-sent sword, a god-sent crow, and the treachery of earthly chieftains turned against themselves, while local earth-deities line the route as willing retainers of the heavenly descendant.

functions: Legitimates the imperial line's eastward conquest as a divine mandate delivered by Amaterasu and Takamimusubi through dream-oracles, the quelling-sword of Takemikazuchi, and the guiding sun-crow.
Provides the sacred biography behind the yatagarasu (three-legged crow) emblem of the Kumano shrines and the solar-orientation taboo of the campaign.
Fixes place-names along the expedition route (Tadetsu, Chinu, the river-mouth of Wo, Uda-no-Chihara, Yakidzu of Uda) as memory devices tying the landscape to the dynasty's origins.
Models the conduct of the first sacred king: ritual caution toward deities, reliance on divination and dreams, and singing as command and signal.

variants.name: Nihongi Book III variant (Aston 1896)
variants.text_tradition: Nihongi (Chronicles of Japan), compiled 720 CE, Book III - the expedition told from the second official chronicle with different names and episode order
variants.summary: In the Nihongi the princes sail and sojourn for years before the assault; Nagasune-biko first repulses a vanguard led by Nigi-hayabi, whose master Shinatsu-hiko turns back; Itsuse is wounded in the arm by Nagasune's arrow and speaks the same 'not right to fight facing the sun' lament before dying at the Kii river-mouth; the sword drops through Takakuraji's storehouse in a dream of Futsu-nushi-no-kami acting for Takemikazuchi; the crow Yatagarasu guides the host; and Nagasune is finally shot down in a negotiated encounter after Michi-no-omi's forces land in force.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Jimmu narrative is the founding charter of the Japanese imperial line and was invoked by State Shinto ideology before 1945; treat it as comparative mythology, present the historical problems of the 'first emperor' openly, and avoid devotional or nationalist framing.

title.en: The Divine Arrow-Lord of Miwa and Jimmu's Empress
title.zh: 三輪山大物主化箭求婚與伊須氣余理比賣

region.en: Mount Miwa and the moor of Takasazhi, Yamato (Nara plain)

summary.en: Seeking a chief empress, Jimmu is told of a maiden called the august child of a Deity: the Great-Master-of-Things deity of Miwa admired the beautiful Seya-datarahime, transformed himself into a red-painted arrow, pierced her, and became a handsome youth who married her; their daughter is I-suke-yori-hime. Jimmu's courtier Ohokume, watching seven maidens play on the Takasazhi moor, picks out I-suke-yori-hime standing first and reports her in song; she answers in astonishment at his slit eyes, and the Heavenly Sovereign goes to her house on the River Sawi to sleep one night before bringing her into the palace.
summary.zh: 神武天皇求正后。三輪山的大物主神慕勢夜陀多良比賣之美，化為丹塗矢，遂成美男子與她成婚，所生女即伊須氣余理比賣，故稱神女。大久米命於高倉野見七少女遊戲，唱歌辨出立於最前者，天皇遂幸其河背之家一夜，納入後宮。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the arrow-conception episode is paraphrased from the translator's Latin rendering of the original; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, ruling at Kashibara, sought a beautiful maiden to make his Chief Empress, his commander Ohokume told him of a beauteous girl in Yamato who was called the august child of a Deity, and explained the name. The Princess Seya-datarahime, daughter of Mizokuhi of Mishima, was admired for her beauty by the Great-Master-of-Things, the Deity of Miwa. The god changed himself into an arrow painted red, transfixed her by the privy, and startled her: she fled, then brought the arrow home and laid it beside her bed. Suddenly it became a handsome young man, who swiftly joined the beautiful girl to himself in marriage; their daughter was named Hoto-tatara-i-susugi-hime - the same as Hime-tatara-i-suke-yori-hime. So therefore she is called the august child of a Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 232-233 (1882); the original's arrow-courtship lines are here translated in Latin and rendered back into English; not verbatim.

passages.text: Seven beauteous maidens were playing on the moor of Takasazhi, and I-suke-yori-hime stood among them. Ohokume, seeing her, spoke to the Heavenly Sovereign in a song pointing her out among the maidens; the Sovereign, reading in his heart that the girl standing in the very front was the one, replied with a song of his own. When Ohokume carried the Sovereign's decree to her, she sang back in astonishment at the courtier's slit eyes, and he sang an answer explaining himself. So the maiden promised she would respectfully serve the Heavenly Sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 233-234 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The maiden's house stood on the bank of the River Sawi. The Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to her dwelling and slept there one august night; afterwards I-suke-yori-hime came and entered the palace, and the Sovereign sang at her arrival. The children born of this marriage were Hiko-ya-wi, Kamu-ya-wi-mimi, and Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi - the last to reign as the second sovereign of the line.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 234-235 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Tagishi-mimi's Plot and the Sword of Suizei
title.zh: 手研耳命之陰謀與綏靖天皇即位

region.en: Palaces of Unebi-Kashibara and Takawoka in Kadzuraki, Yamato (Nara plain)
region.zh: 畝傍與葛城高丸宮（大和）

summary.en: After Jimmu's death his elder half-brother Tagishi-mimi marries the Empress I-suke-yori-hime and plots to slay her three young sons. The mother laments and betrays the plot through songs; the eldest prince Kamu-ya-wi-mimi takes up a weapon but trembles so that he cannot strike, and his younger brother Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi begs for the weapon and slays Tagishi-mimi himself. Praised for the deed as Take-nuna-kaha-mimi, he is ceded the sovereignty by the elder brother, who resolves to serve him as a priest: thus the valiant slayer, not the firstborn, reigns as the Emperor Suizei.
summary.zh: 神武天皇崩後，異母兄手研耳命娶皇后伊須氣余理比賣，謀殺三位年幼皇子。母后哀慟，以歌示警。長子神八井耳命持兵欲誅之，然手足顫抖不能下手；弟神渾名河耳命乞劍親往誅手研耳，遂稱建沼河耳命。長兄以弟勇而讓位，自任祭祀輔佐，弟即位為綏靖天皇。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko, who had lived one hundred and thirty-seven years and been buried on the Kashi spur by Mount Unebi, his elder half-brother Tagishi-mimi wedded the Empress I-suke-yori-hime. Pending his design he plotted how he might slay his three younger brethren, the sons of Jimmu; and their august mother, lamenting, made the plot known to her children through a song, singing it once and then again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 235-236 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hearing the song, her august children knew their danger and resolved to slay Tagishi-mimi first. The elder prince Kamu-ya-wi-mimi said to his younger brother Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi: do you take a weapon and go in and slay Tagishi-mimi. The elder prince took a weapon, went in, and made ready to slay him; but his arms and legs trembled so that he was unable. Then the younger brother begged for the weapon his elder brother held, went in himself, and slew Tagishi-mimi. In praise of the deed the younger brother was again named Take-nuna-kaha-mimi, the Valiant of Nunakaha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 236-237 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kamu-ya-wi-mimi then resigned the sovereignty to the younger brother: I could not slay the foeman, he said, but Thine Augustness was at once able to slay him. Though I be the elder, it is not right that I should be the superior; wherefore do you be the superior and rule all beneath the heaven, while I become a priest and respectfully serve you. So the slayer of Tagishi-mimi, though the younger, took the throne and ruled the Empire - the sovereign the chronicles count as Emperor Suizei, who dwelt at the palace of Takawoka in Kadzuraki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 237-239 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Emperor Sujin's Dream Oracle and Ō-tataneko the Priest of Miwa
title.zh: 崇神天皇夢兆與大田田根子祭三輪神

region.en: Palace of Midzugaki at Shiki and Mount Mimoro (Miwa), Yamato (Nara plain)
region.zh: 磯城瑞籬宮與三輪山（大和）

summary.en: In Sujin's reign a great pestilence kills the people as if none were to be left. In a dream the Great-Master-of-Things deity declares the plague his own doing and demands worship through Ō-tataneko, a man then unknown. Couriers search the empire and find him in the village of Minu in Kafuchi; asked whose child he is, he recites a divine pedigree running back through Takemikazuchi to Ōmononushi and Iku-tama-yori-bime. Rejoiced, the emperor makes him high-priest of the Great Deity of Great Miwa on Mount Mimoro, establishes eighty platters of offerings and shrines with red and black shields and spears, and the pestilential vapour ceases and the land is tranquilized.
summary.zh: 崇神天皇時大疫，民幾死盡。夜夢大物主大神言：此乃我所為；若以大田田根子祭我，則神意平息，國土安寧。使者遍尋，於河內美努村得之。天皇問其出身，大田田根子自述其世系出自建御雷神，遠祖為大物主神與玉依比賣。天皇大喜，立之為三輪山神主，造八十甌饌、建神社，以丹盾矛祭狹山神、以黑盾矛祭大坂神，瘟氣遂止，天下太平。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the reign of the Heavenly Sovereign Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe (Emperor Sujin) a great pestilence arose, and the people died as if none were to be left. The Sovereign grieved and lamented, and at night, on his divine couch, there appeared to him in a dream the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things, who said: this pestilence is my august doing. If you will cause me to be worshipped by the man Ō-tataneko, my divine spirit shall not arise again, and the land will be tranquillized. No one knew where such a man was to be found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 261-262 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Couriers were dispatched in every direction to search for Ō-tataneko, and he was discovered in the village of Minu in Kafuchi and respectfully brought before the Sovereign. Asked whose child he was, he replied with his pedigree: I am Ō-tataneko, child of His Augustness Takemikazuchi, who was child of Ihi-gata-sumi, child of Kushi-mi-gata, child of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things by his wife Iku-tama-yori-bime, daughter of Suwe-tsu-mimi. The Heavenly Sovereign, greatly rejoiced, commanded that the Empire should be tranquil and the people flourish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 262 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sovereign made Ō-tataneko high-priest to worship the Great Deity of Great Miwa on Mount Mimoro. He further ordered Igaka-shiko-wo to make eighty heavenly platters and reverently establish the shrines of the Heavenly Deities and the Earthly Deities; to worship the Deity of Sumisaka at Uda with a red-coloured shield and spear, and the Deity of Ohosaka with a black-coloured shield and spear; and to present august offerings of cloth to all the deities of the declivities of the hills and of the reaches of the rivers, neglecting none. In consequence the pestilential vapour ceased altogether, and the country was tranquillized.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 262-263 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Red Earth and the Thread: Iku-tama-yori-bime and the Night God of Miwa
title.zh: 紅土穿針：玉依比賣與三輪山神之婚

region.en: Mount Miwa shrine, Yamato (Nara plain) (symbolic pin for the god's nocturnal visits)
region.zh: 三輪山神社（大和）（夜訪情節之象徵性定位）

summary.en: The maiden Iku-tama-yori-bime is so beautiful that a divine youth begins visiting her every night, and she grows pregnant without knowing his name. Her startled parents teach her a tracking rite: sprinkle red earth before the couch and pierce the hem of his garment with a needle threaded with hemp. In the morning the thread runs out through the door-hook hole, and only three twists of hemp remain; following the thread up Mount Miwa, it stops at the shrine of the deity. Thus the child Ō-tataneko is proved the god's, and the place is called Miwa - 'three twists'.
summary.zh: 少女玉依比賣容姿端麗，神妙之童子每夜自來相會，遂未婚而孕。父母驚問，女言不知其名之童子夜夜相伴。父母授計：榻前撒紅土，以麻線穿針縫其衣裾。翌晨麻線穿過門鉤孔而出，僅餘三結。循線追至三輪山，線止於神社，方知其子為神所生。此地遂名三輪（三結）——後世大物主大神之御子大田田根子由此得證。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Iku-tama-yori-bime was regularly beautiful, whereupon a divine youth, judging her majesty of appearance without comparison in the world, came suddenly to her in the middle of the night. Loving each other, they lived together in matrimony, and ere long the maiden was pregnant. Her astonished father and mother asked: thou art pregnant by thyself - how art thou with child without having known a man? She replied: I have naturally conceived through a beautiful young man whose name I know not; he comes every evening and stays with me.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 263-264 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wishing to know who the man was, her parents instructed their daughter: sprinkle red earth in front of the couch, and pass a skein of hemp through a needle, and pierce with it the skirt of his garment. She did as they had told her. In the morning, the needle's hemp had gone out through the hole of the door-hook, and of all the hemp only three twists remained: the night visitor had made his escape through the hook-hole, trailing the thread behind him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 264 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The family followed the thread on its quest. It ran and ran until, reaching Mount Miwa, it stopped at the shrine of the Deity that dwelt there. So they knew that the child in the maiden's womb was the child of that god, and in time Ō-tataneko was born - the man whom the pestilence-dream of Emperor Sujin would later name as the only fitting priest of the Great Deity of Miwa. The place itself took its name from the three twists of hemp that remained: Miwa, the Three Twists.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 264 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Vanishing Songstress and Take-hani-yasu's Rebellion
title.zh: 隱沒歌女預言與武埴安彥之亂

region.en: Pass of Hera in Yamashiro and the River Wakara (south of Kyoto) (approximate pin)
region.zh: 山代平坂與和訶羅河（京都以南）（約略定位）

summary.en: Emperor Sujin sends his generals out to pacify the circuits; as Ōbiko rides toward Koshi, a girl in a loin-skirt stands on the Pass of Hera singing a song that speaks of the Great Yamato being ruled by one true lord, then vanishes into thin air. Taking the song as an omen, the emperor charges Ōbiko with the half-brother Take-hani-yasu's plot in Yamashiro. Setting sacred jars on the Pass of Wani, the imperial army faces Take-hani-yasu across the River Wakara; the rebels' first arrow misses, Hiko-kuni-buku's answer strikes the rebel king dead, and the rout leaves its marks in place-names from Kusobakama to the Cormorant River.
summary.zh: 崇神天皇遣大彥命等巡撫四方。大彥命赴越國途中，山代平坂有系裙少女歌曰：「真若我王，御國統治」，言畢忽而不見。天皇斷為兄武埴安彥謀反之兆，命討之。在和邇坂置神甌，兩軍隔和訶羅河對峙；彥五瀨武先射不中，彥國葺一箭斃武埴安彥，叛軍潰散。追擊至草鹿堀，逃者矢被褌（草袴），地名由來；屍浮如鸕鶿，河名鵜川；斬戮之地名幡田野。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In this reign the Heavenly Sovereign sent Ōbiko to the circuit of Koshi, his son Take-nunakaha-wake to the twelve circuits eastward, and Hiko-imasu to Taniha to slay Kugamimi. As Ōbiko was going away to Koshi, a young girl wearing a loin-skirt stood on the Pass of Hera in Yamashiro and sang a song; thinking it strange, Ōbiko turned his horse back and asked what the words meant. The girl answered: I said nothing; I was only singing a song - and thereupon she suddenly vanished, none could see whither.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 265-266 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ōbiko returned to the capital and reported the matter. The Heavenly Sovereign read the omen: methinks this is a sign that my half-brother, King Take-hani-yasu, who dwells in the land of Yamashiro, is planning some foul plot; do you, uncle, raise an army and go after him. Joined by Hiko-kuni-buku, Ōbiko set sacred jars on the Pass of Wani and marched. When they reached the River Wakara in Yamashiro, Take-hani-yasu, who had raised an army, was waiting to intercept the passage, and the two hosts stood confronting and challenging each other across the water; the place took its name, Idomi, from the standoff.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 266-267 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hiko-kuni-buku begged the enemy to let fly the first arrow. Take-hani-yasu shot, but could not strike; then Kuni-buku's arrow flew and struck the rebel king dead on the spot. His whole army was routed and fled in confusion. Harassed in the pursuit to the ferry of Kusuba, the fugitives' excrement clung to their breeches, whence the place is named Kusobakama; cut down where they were intercepted, their bodies floated like cormorants in the river, and the river was called U-kaha, the Cormorant River; and because the warriors were cut to pieces there, the field is called Hafuri-sono. Having finished the work of pacification, the generals went up to make their report, and the empire was at peace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 267 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Homutsu-wake the Mute Prince and the Swan Sent from Izumo
title.zh: 本牟智和氣啞王子與出雲大神之咒

region.en: Yamato to Izumo: the River Hi and the shrine of the Great Deity of Idzumo (symbolic pin on the Izumo shrine)
region.zh: 大和至出雲：斐川與出雲大社（象徵性定位）

summary.en: Emperor Suinin's son Homutsu-wake, though his beard reached his belly, never spoke a word. At his first cry after a swan's cry the emperor sends a pursuer who chases the bird through province after province and nets it at last in the estuary of Wanami in Koshi - yet the prince still does not speak. A dream bids the emperor build a temple like his own abode; divination reveals the curse is the doing of the Great Deity of Idzumo. After a sworn oath-heron falls dead and revives to prove the envoy Ake-tatsu's worth, the prince is sent to worship at Izumo, and there, before an imitation green-leafed mountain of food, he speaks for the first time - recognizing the offering of the deity's priest. A serpent-bride and a panicky flight home complete the tale.
summary.zh: 垂仁天皇皇子本牟智和氣雖鬚及胸而不語。聞白鳥之聲始發一言，天皇遣山背之大高逐鳥，追經播磨、因幡、丹波、但馬、近江、美濃、尾張、信濃至越，於和田奈湊張網捕得，王子仍不語。帝夢告：為我建如御殿之社，王子必能言。占卜知乃出雲大神之咒。明石浦誓約之鷺死而復生，證明阿岐豆王使者之誠。王子赴出雲參拜，於模仿青山之前忽然說話，辨認大物主神社禰宜之御食。後王子夜娶日香姬，見其為蛇而逃，姬光照海原乘船追趕，一行攏船越山而逃回大和。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Suinin (Ikume-iri-biko-isachi) amused his mute son with a two-forked boat made of a two-forked cryptomeria from Ahidzu in Wohari, floated on the pools of Ichishi and Karu in Yamato: the august child, though his eight-grasp beard reached to the pit of his stomach, spoke never a word. Then, hearing the cry of a high-flying swan, he made his first utterance. The Heavenly Sovereign sent Yamanobe-no-Ohotaka to catch the bird, and the man pursued the swan from the land of Ki through Harima and Inaba, Taniha and Tajima, round eastward to Afumi, Minu, Wohari and Shinanu, until in the land of Koshi he spread a net in the estuary of Wanami, caught the bird, and brought it up to the capital. But the prince, seeing the bird again, still did not speak as had been hoped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 278-279 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sovereign, grieved, fell asleep and was instructed in a dream: if thou wilt build my temple like unto thine august abode, the august child shall surely speak. Grand divination was made to learn what deity's desire this might be, and it was discovered that the curse was the august doing of the Great Deity of Idzumo. King Ake-tatsu was chosen to attend the prince, and proved by oath: if there is truly to be an answer to our adoration, may the heron dwelling by the Pool of Sagisu fall dead - and the heron fell dead, and at his command came to life again; likewise a bear-oak on Cape Amakashi withered and revived at his oath. Divination of the starting-gate showed the Ki gate lucky, and the prince set out with attendants who established the Homuji clan in every place they arrived at.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 279-281 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At Izumo they finished worshipping the Great Deity and made a black plaited bridge in the middle of the River Hi, offering a temporary palace for the prince. There the ruler of the land of Idzumo, Kihisa-tsu-mi, made an imitation green-leafed mountain and set it in the lower reach of the river to present the great august food. At the sight the prince spoke for the first time: what there resembles a green-leafed mountain looks like a mountain, but is not a mountain - is it perchance the great court of the deacon who holds in reverence the Great Deity Ugly-Male-of-the-Reed-Plains that dwells in the temple of So at Ihakuma in Idzumo? The attendant kings, hearing with joy and seeing with delight, settled the prince in the palace of Nagaho at Ajimasa and sent a courier up to report that the child could now speak through the worship of the Great Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 281-282 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince wedded Princess Hinaga for one night; looking privately at the beautiful maiden, he found her a serpent, and fled away alarmed. Princess Hinaga, vexed, illuminated the sea-plain and pursued the fugitives in a ship; more and more terrified, they pulled their august vessel across the mountain-folds and so escaped up to the capital. There they reported why they had come: the great august child had become able to speak through worshipping the Great Deity. The delighted Sovereign sent King Unakami back to build the deity's temple, and on account of the child established the Totori clan, the Torikahi clan, the Homuji clan, and the Ohoyuwe and Wakayuwe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 282-283 (1882); not verbatim.

title.zh: 被遣返的丹波公主之悲

region.en: Sagaraka in Yamashiro and the deep pool of Otokuni (south of Kyoto) (approximate pin)
region.zh: 山代狭木坂與乙訓深淵（京都以南）（約略定位）

summary.en: Summoning the four daughters of Prince Tatasu-michi-no-ushi of Taniha, Suinin keeps the two elder, Hibasu and Oto, as consorts, but sends the two younger, Utakori and Matonu, back to their native place for their extreme hideousness. Humiliated before the neighbouring villages, Princess Matonu tries to hang herself from a tree-branch at Sagaraka in Yamashiro - giving the place its name - and finally drowns herself in a deep pool at Otokuni, which becomes Ochikuni, the 'fallen pool'.
summary.zh: 垂仁天皇召丹波道主王四女：留日穗姬與弟姬為妃，以二妹鳥兒與沼名兒貌醜而遣歸鄉。沼名兒羞於近鄰知其被棄，至山代狹木坂，欲縊於樹枝，故其地稱狹木坂；至乙訓，終投深淵而死，故其地稱落國（乙訓）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In accordance with the Empress's words, the Heavenly Sovereign summoned four princesses, the daughters of Prince Tatasu-michi-no-ushi of Taniha: Princess Hibasu, Princess Oto, Princess Utakori, and Princess Matonu. He kept the two, Hibasu and Oto; but the two younger queens he sent back to their native place on account of their extreme hideousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 283-284 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Princess Matonu spoke in her mortification: when it is known in the neighbouring villages that among sisters of one family we two were sent back for our ugliness, the shame will be beyond bearing. On reaching Sagaraka in the land of Yamashiro she tried to kill herself by hanging from the branch of a tree, so the place was called Sagariki. Again, on reaching Otokuni, she at last killed herself by jumping into a deep pool; so that place was called Ochikuni - the place now named Otokuni.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 284 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Tajima-mori and the Orange of the Eternal Land

region.en: Yamato court and the Eternal Land (Tokoyo) across the sea (symbolic pin on the Yamato court; Tokoyo itself is otherworldly)
region.zh: 大和宮廷與海外常世國（常世為異界，象徵性定位）

summary.en: Emperor Suinin sends Tajima-mori, ancestor of the Chiefs of Miyake, to the Eternal Land to fetch the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree. Tajima-mori reaches that country, plucks the fruit, and returns with his burden to find the emperor dead in the meantime. He sets part of the fruit before the Great Empress Hibasu and part as an offering at the door of the imperial mausoleum; then, raising the fruit of the tree on high and wailing, 'Bringing the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree from the Eternal Land, I have come to serve thee', he weeps himself to death at the grave. That fruit, the record says, is what is now called the orange.
summary.zh: 垂仁天皇遣三宅首祖田島守赴常世國求常世長鳴木之果。田島守至彼國摘果而歸，然天皇已崩。乃以四枝獻太后日穗姬，四枝供於帝陵門前；高舉果枝慟哭曰：「持常世長鳴木之果，來奉侍天皇」，遂哭死於陵前。其果即今之橘。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign sent Tajima-mori, ancestor of the Chiefs of Miyake, to the Eternal Land to fetch the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree - the fruit, men said, that never fades and never loses its scent. Tajima-mori at last reached that country beyond the sea, plucked the fruit of the tree, and set out home with his treasure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 284 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: But meanwhile the Heavenly Sovereign had died. Tajima-mori set apart four branches of clubmoss and four of spears to present to the Great Empress, and four of each as an offering at the door of the Heavenly Sovereign's august mausoleum. Then, raising on high the fruit of the tree, he wailed and wept: Bringing the fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree from the Eternal Land, I have come to serve thee! - and at last he wailed and wept himself to death at the grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 284-285 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign himself lived one hundred and fifty-three years, and his mausoleum lies in the middle of the moor of Mitachi at Sugahara. In the time of the Great Empress Hibasu the Stone-Coffin-Makers' corporation and the Earthenware-Masters' clan were established, and she was buried in the mausoleum of Terama near Saki. And the fruit that Tajima-mori mourned with is, says the record, what is now called the orange: the first tachibana of Japan, brought home from the land of no death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 285-286 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ōho-usu Steals the Maidens of Minu

region.en: Palace of Hishiro at Makimuku, Yamato (Nara plain)

summary.en: To assure himself of the beauty of the two maidens Ye-hime and Oto-tsube, daughters of King Kamu-oho-ne of Minu, Emperor Keikō sends his son Ōho-usu to summon them to the capital. The prince instead wedds both maidens himself, then sends up other women under their names. The emperor knows them for substitutes, subjects them to long glances but never weds them, leaving them to sorrow; the elder brother keeps the two sons he has founded, Ōshikuro-no-ye-hiko and Ōshikuro-no-oto-hiko.
summary.zh: 景行天皇聞美濃國主鏡王之女兄姬、弟姬美名，遣皇子大碓命召入京。大碓命竟自娶二女，另以他女冒名獻上。天皇明知其非，屢屢注視而終不娶，令其悲傷。大碓命與二女所生者，即黑兄彥王與黑弟彥王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign, wishing to assure himself of what he had heard of the beauty of the two maidens Ye-hime and Oto-tsube, daughters of King Kamu-oho-ne, ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Minu, sent his august son Ōho-usu to summon them up to the capital. The prince who had been sent did not summon them: instead he forthwith wedded both the maidens himself, and then sought out other women, to whom he falsely gave the maidens' names, and sent them up in their place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 290-291 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign knew the women he received for substitutes. He frequently subjected them to his long glances, but never wedding them he caused them to sorrow. From the stolen marriage, however, two princes survived the scandal: Ōshikuro-no-ye-hiko, son of Ye-hime, and Ōshikuro-no-oto-hiko, son of Oto-tsube. In this reign too the Labourers' Tribe and the Great Butlers' Tribe were established, the port of Aha in the East, the granaries of Yamato, and the Pool of Sakate with bamboos planted on its bank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 291-292 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-takeru in the Cave of the Kumaso Bravoes
title.zh: 日本武尊熊襲洞窟之計

region.zh: 熊襲之地，筑紫（象徵性定位）

summary.en: When Keikō asks his son Wo-usu why the prince's elder brother never comes to meals, the boy coolly confesses that he crushed and dismembered him in the privy. Alarmed at his child's ferocity, the emperor sends him west against the two Kumaso bravoes. Wo-usu takes his aunt Yamato-hime's silk garments, hides a sabre in his bosom, combs his hair like a girl, and lets the enemy set him between them at their feast; at the feast's height he stabs the elder through the chest and the younger through the buttock. The dying Kumaso, learning who he is, names him Yamato-take - braver than any man in the West - before the prince rips him open like a ripe melon.
summary.zh: 景行天皇問小碓命：兄何不朝夕饍？小碓答：晨間入廁時扼殺之，拔其手足，以蓆裹而棄之。天皇驚其暴烈，乃命西討熊襲雙梟帥。倭姬授御衣御裳，小碓藏劍於懷，束髮如少女，混入慶宴立於二梟帥之間。宴至酣處，抽劍刺兄梟帥之胸，追弟梟帥刺其臀。垂死梟帥知其身份後曰：西方無人比我兄弟之勇，然大和有更勇者，願獻尊名：自今當稱日本武尊。言畢即被剖如熟瓜而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), primary-source version of an episode also told from Davis (1912) in japanese-yamato-takeru-kumaso; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign said to Wo-usu: why does not thine elder brother come forth to the morning and evening great repasts? Be thou the one to teach him his duty. For five days the prince still came not forth. Asked how he had taken the trouble, Wo-usu answered coolly: in the early morning, when he went into the privy, I grasped hold of him and crushed him, and, pulling off his limbs, wrapped them in matting and flung them away. Alarmed at the valour and ferocity of his son's disposition, the Sovereign commanded him: in the West there are two Kumaso bravoes, unsubmissive and disrespectful men; so take them - and sent him off, his hair bound at the brow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 291-292 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His aunt, Her Augustness Yamato-hime, granted the prince her august upper garment and skirt, and with a sabre hidden in his bosom he went forth. Near the Kumaso house a three-fold belt of warriors had made a cave to dwell in, and they were noisily preparing a rejoicing for their august cave. Wo-usu sauntered about the neighbourhood until the day of the feast, when, having combed down his bound hair after the manner of girls and put on his aunt's garment and skirt, he looked quite like a young girl, and standing amidst the women went inside the cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 292-293 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two Kumaso bravoes, delighted at the sight of the maiden, set her between them and rejoiced exuberantly. When the feast was at its height, Wo-usu drew the sabre from his bosom, caught the elder by the collar of his garment and thrust it through his chest. The younger bravo ran out; pursued to the bottom of the steps and caught by the back, he too was stabbed through the buttock - yet he begged: do not move the sword; I have something to say. Who is Thine Augustness? I am, answered the prince, the august child of Ōtarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake who rules the Land of the Eight Great Islands from the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku; my name is King Yamato-wo-guna, and the Sovereign sent me to take and slay you two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 293-294 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Kumaso spoke his praise: that must be true. There are no persons in the West so brave and strong as we two, yet in the Land of Great Yamato there is a man braver than we. Therefore I offer thee an august name: from this time forward it is right that thou be praised as the august child Yamato-take. As soon as he had finished speaking, the prince ripped him up like a ripe melon and slew him. Thenceforward he was praised as His Augustness Yamato-take; and returning to the capital he subdued and pacified every one of the deities of the mountains, the rivers, and Anado on the way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 294 and 297 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-takeru and the Wooden Sword of the Izumo Bravo
title.zh: 日本武尊出雲勇士木劍之計

summary.en: Entering Izumo to slay its bravo, Yamato-takeru first binds himself to him in friendship and secretly has a false sword carved of oak wood, which he girds on. Bathing together in the River Hi, he gets out first, takes up the bravo's real steel, and proposes an exchange of swords; the unsuspecting bravo girds on the wooden one. Yamato-takeru then invites him to cross swords - and the bravo, unable to draw his false blade, is slain, with a song of triumph sung over the deed.
summary.zh: 日本武尊入出雲，欲誅出雲梟帥，先結為友，密令以山栲木造偽劍佩之。與梟帥共浴斐川，武尊先出，取梟帥所置真劍佩上，曰：劍換之！梟帥不知，佩偽木劍而出。武尊曰：來，交劍！梟帥拔偽劍不得出，武尊即拔真劍斬之，遂作歌而誅。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), primary-source version of an episode also told from Davis (1912) in japanese-yamato-takeru-wooden-sword; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Entering the Land of Idzumo with the wish to slay its bravo, Yamato-takeru first bound himself to him in friendship. Secretly he had the wood of an oak made into a false sword, and girded it on. Then he went with the bravo to bathe in the River Hi; and Yamato-takeru, getting out of the river first, took up the sword the Izumo bravo had taken off and laid down, girded it on himself, and said: let us exchange swords!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 294-295 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards the Izumo bravo got out of the river and girded on Yamato-takeru's false sword, suspecting nothing. Come on, said Yamato-takeru, let us cross swords! But when the bravo tried to draw, the false sword would not leave its sheath; and Yamato-takeru, drawing his own steel, slew him on the bank, singing a song of triumph over the deed. So having extirpated the bravoes and made the land orderly, he went up to the capital and made his report to the Heavenly Sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 295 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Herb-Quelling Sabre and the Burning Moor of Sagamu

region.zh: 駿河之野（東海道）（約略定位）

summary.en: Ordered east a second time without an army, Yamato-takeru tells his aunt Yamato-hime at Ise that the emperor must think he will die quickly; weeping, he receives from her the Herb-Quelling-Sabre and a closed bag - open the mouth of the bag, she says, if there be an emergency. After plighting troth with Princess Miyadzu of Wohari for his return, he reaches Sagamu, whose ruler lies that a violent deity dwells in a lagoon and then fires the moor with the prince inside it. Opening the bag, Yamato-takeru finds a fire-striker: he mows the grass with the sabre, strikes counter-fire, burns the fire back, escapes, and kills and burns every ruler of the land, whence the place is called Yakidzu.
summary.zh: 景行天皇再遣日本武尊東討十二國，不與軍隊。武尊入伊勢神宮拜其姑倭姬，泣言：父皇必以為我速死，西討甫歸，不賜兵復遣東征。倭姬乃賜草薙劍并一口袋：有急，開袋口。至尾張，與宮簀媛約婚而後東行，平山川諸神。至駿河，國造詭言野中有神，武尊入野視之，國造縱火燒野。尊啟袋，得打火具；乃以劍刈草，打出火，反燒其火而退，盡殺國造等縱火者，其地遂名燒津。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), primary-source version of an episode also told from Davis (1912) in japanese-yamato-takeru-grass-sword; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign again urged his command on Yamato-take: subdue and pacify the savage deities and the unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East - and sent him off joined to Prince Mi-suki-tomo-mimi-take, ancestor of the Grandees of Kibi, bestowing on him a holly-wood spear eight fathoms long. Entering the temple of the Great August Deity of Ise, he worshipped and spoke to his aunt Yamato-hime: it must surely be that the Heavenly Sovereign thinks I may die quickly; for after sending me to smite the wicked people of the West, I am no sooner come up again than, without bestowing on me an army, he sends me off afresh to pacify the twelve circuits of the East. Departing with lamentations and tears, he received from her the Herb-Quelling-Sabre and likewise an august bag, with the words: if there should be an emergency, open the mouth of the bag.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 295-296 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Reaching the Land of Wohari, he went into the house of Princess Miyadzu, ancestress of the Rulers of Wohari; thinking to wed her at once, he instead plighted his troth, promising to wed her when he should return from the East, and went on into the Eastern Lands, subduing and pacifying all the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the mountains and rivers. Then he reached the Land of Sagamu, whose Ruler lied to him: in the middle of this moor is a great lagoon, and the Deity that dwells in the middle of the lagoon is a very violent Deity.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 296-297 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yamato-take entered the moor to see the deity - and the Ruler of the land set fire to the moor all around him. Knowing himself deceived, the prince opened the mouth of the bag his aunt had bestowed and found inside it a fire-striker. He first mowed away the herbage with his august sword, took the fire-striker, struck out fire, and kindling a counter-fire burnt the herbage against the other fire, driving the flames back; then he returned forth, killed and destroyed all the Rulers of that land, and set fire to and burnt them. So that place is now called Yakidzu - the place of burning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 297 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Oto-tachibana Enters the Sea to Calm the Waves

region.en: Sea of Hashiri-midzu, Sagami Bay (approximate pin off the Kanagawa coast)
region.zh: 走水海，相模灣（神奈川外海）（約略定位）

summary.en: Crossing the sea of Hashiri-midzu on his eastern campaign, Yamato-takeru's ship is tossed by the Deity of the crossing so that it cannot proceed. His empress, Princess Oto-tachibana, declares she will enter the sea in his place so that the mission may be completed, spreads eight thicknesses of sedge rugs, of skin rugs and of silk rugs on the waves, and sits down on the top of them; the violent waves at once go down and the ship passes on. Seven days later her august comb drifts ashore, and the men take it and bury it in a mausoleum made for it.
summary.zh: 日本武尊東征渡走水海，海神興浪，船不得進。后弟橘媛曰：妾願代皇子入海，皇子務須完成東征使命，奏報天皇。乃於波上敷八重草蓆、八重皮蓆、八重絹蓆，坐於其上，浪即平息，船遂得渡。七日後，后之御櫛漂著海濱，乃取之葬於所造之御陵。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki), primary-source version of an episode also told from Davis (1912) in japanese-ototachibana-sacrifice; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When Yamato-take thence penetrated on and crossed the sea of Hashiri-midzu, the Deity of that crossing raised the waves, tossing the ship so that it could not proceed across. Then the prince's empress, Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana, spoke: I will enter the sea instead of the august child. The august child must complete the service on which he has been sent, and take back a report to the Heavenly Sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 298 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When she was about to enter the sea, she spread eight thicknesses of sedge rugs, eight thicknesses of skin rugs, and eight thicknesses of silk rugs on the top of the waves, and sat down on the top of them. Thereupon the violent waves at once went down, and the august ship was able to proceed. She sang her farewell as the waters took her; and seven days afterwards the empress's august comb drifted onto the sea-beach, where it was taken and placed in an august mausoleum that was made for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 298-299 (1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Deer of Ashigara and the Old Man's Song in Kahi
title.zh: 足柄坂白鹿與甲斐老翁續歌

region.en: Ashigara Pass and the palace of Sakawori in Kahi (Kai) (approximate pin)
region.zh: 足柄坂與甲斐佐久疑宮（約略定位）

summary.en: Returning west after subduing the savage Yemishi and the mountain and river deities, Yamato-takeru stops to eat at the foot of the Ashigara Pass, where the pass deity confronts him transformed into a white deer; a scrap of wild chive thrown at its eye strikes it dead. From the top of the pass he sighs three times, 'Adzuma ha ya!' - Oh, my wife! - grieving for the drowned Oto-tachibana, and the eastern land takes its name, Adzuma, from the cry. Crossing into Kahi and dwelling in the palace of Sakawori, he sings; the old man who lights his fire completes the song, and Yamato-takeru rewards him with the rulership of the Eastern Lands.
summary.zh: 日本武尊平定蝦夷、山川諸神後西歸，足柄坂下用膳，坂神化身白鹿而立，尊以山韭擊其目而斃之。登坂頂三嘆曰：「吾妻者耶！」（悼弟橘媛），東國遂名阿豆摩（吾妻）。入甲斐佐久疑宮而歌，主炊老翁續歌而成，尊嘉之，賜東國國造之位。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Having thence penetrated on and subdued all the savage Yemishi, and likewise pacified all the savage deities of the mountains and rivers, Yamato-takeru was returning up to the capital. On reaching the foot of the Ashigara Pass he was eating his august provisions when the Deity of the pass, transformed into a white deer, came and stood before him. Forthwith, waiting and striking the deer with a scrap of wild chive, he hit it in the eye and struck it dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. p. 299 (1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mounting to the top of the pass, he sighed three times and spoke: Adzuma ha ya! - Oh, my wife! - mourning the empress who had entered the sea for him; and so that land east of the pass is called by the name of Adzuma. Crossing over from that land into Kahi, he dwelt in the palace of Sakawori and sang a song; and the old man who was the lighter of the august fire completed the august song for him, singing it through to the end. Yamato-takeru praised the old man and forthwith bestowed on him the rulership of the Eastern Land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Chamberlain trans. pp. 300 (1882); not verbatim.
